## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

# Claudinite work-item executor (tasks-dispatch DESIGN §6, §10) — a pull worker
# over the queue. ONE RUN DRAINS THE QUEUE (§15.30, reversing §15.22's one-item
# run): Actions bills each job's minutes rounded up, so a run per item paid a
# whole invocation — checkout, setup, rounding — for each one. A run now settles
# its items one at a time until nothing is pickable, and the continuation job
# below covers a run that dies mid-drain. It carries NO cron of its own — the
# scheduler run's hourly dispatch, made when that run leaves something pickable,
# is the guaranteed delivery, so a lost `task:ready` label event is latency lost
# and never work lost.
#
# THIS IS THE ONLY PLACE SECRETS LIVE (DESIGN §14). The wiring converge stamps
# every task's declared `required_secrets`, plus each configured invocation
# endpoint's token secret, into the step env below by name — the scheduler run and the
# janitor get none, because they never execute task code. Code-work is the only task
# code that ever sees a value; the agent hop carries nothing.
#
# MORE CAPACITY IS MORE EXECUTORS. Nothing enumerates them and each claim is
# independently leased, so a second job, a matrix width, or a runner outside
# Actions entirely all work — the executor's whole interface is issue read/write
# plus the repo at HEAD.
name: Claudinite executor

on:
  issues:
    types: [labeled]
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      continuation_depth:
        description: 'How many dead runs this chain has continued through — set by the continuation job below, never by hand'
        required: false
        type: string

permissions:
  contents: write
  issues: write
  pull-requests: write
  actions: write

jobs:
  execute:
    # A label event on anything else is not this workflow's business — and a
    # workflow_dispatch carries no label at all, so it always runs.
    # BOTH READY SPELLINGS, for as long as any fielded engine writes the legacy one
    # (#1119). A workflow's event trigger names label strings LITERALLY — nothing
    # here decodes — so this list is the one place the migration's two vocabularies
    # must both appear, and dropping the legacy spelling early makes every item an
    # older engine readies wait for the hourly scheduler run instead of starting now.
    if: >-
      github.event_name == 'workflow_dispatch'
      || github.event.label.name == 'task:status:waiting-for-executor'
...
# Claudinite work-item queue — the generator's scheduler run and its drain (tasks-dispatch
# DESIGN §5, §10). This is the repo's ONLY cron, and it replaces the slot
# scheduler's content at the same path when `taskScheduler.dispatch` is `"queue"`
# — same file, same hashed minute, different mechanism, so the one-cron rule and
# every reader that knows this workflow by name keep holding.
#
# A thin shim: all logic lives in the vendored engine, so this file changes
# rarely. The cron line below is a placeholder; bootstrap and the wiring converge
# rewrite it to this repo's stable hashed minute in :10–:50 and its own two
# anchor hours, computed by
# `node .claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/hash-minute.mjs <owner/repo>`.
#
# TWO TICKS A DAY, NOT TWENTY-FOUR (DESIGN §17). Actions bills each job's minutes
# rounded up, so a day's cost is the RUN COUNT — a scheduler run's median is 32
# seconds, and an hourly cron billed 24 minutes a day per repo to do about 13
# minutes of work. The hours are the repo's `taskScheduler.dailyHour` and twelve
# hours after it: the first covers every occurrence the calendar can produce
# (every daily, weekly and monthly anchor falls on that hour), the second carries
# the work that has no anchor — adopting an issue somebody marked, releasing a
# `Not-before`, reclaiming a dead claim. A missed tick costs latency and never an
# occurrence: dueness is read from the anchor, never from whether the cron fired.
#
# TWO JOBS, IN ORDER, THE SECOND CONDITIONAL. The scheduler run is pure label mechanics over the issue list —
# instantiate each task's standing item at its anchor, ready what is due, reclaim
# dead executor claims — and evaluates no precondition and collects no signal. The
# drain then STARTS an executor run for what the scheduler run just created, which is what
# keeps the common case's latency at zero even with no `labeled` event delivered.
# Lost events are therefore never the only delivery — they are latency sugar,
# which is what retires the re-arm.
#
# THE DRAIN RUNS ONLY WHEN THERE IS SOMETHING TO DRAIN (DESIGN §15.30). Actions
# bills each job's minutes rounded up, so an executor dispatched into an empty
# queue costs a full invocation to find nothing: on a quiet repo, 24 of them a
# day. The scheduler-run job reports what it left pickable and the drain job's
# `if` reads it. This weakens no delivery — what a lost label event would have
# delivered is exactly what that parting look sees.
#
# The drain dispatches rather than executes, and that is the point: this workflow's
# concurrency group serializes SCHEDULER RUNS, and an executor run inside it would make each
# hour's scheduler run queue behind the previous hour's work — which the heartbeat, by making
# long work legal, turned from theoretical into likely (DESIGN §15.16).
#
# `workflow_dispatch` is not a convenience: it is the never-wait-for-the-cron
# lever every forced run, migration and validation burst depends on. Its one
# input is how that lever reaches ACROSS repos: the fleet enforcer dispatches
# this workflow naming the tasks to run now, and this member wakes its own
# standing items with its own token (DESIGN §8). The alternative — the enforcer
# editing every member's issues directly — would widen the fleet PAT to issue
# writes on every repository, for a job the member can do for itself.
name: Claudinite scheduler

1	# Working guide — vessel image analysis (rules & conventions)
2	
3	> **Read this before doing any image work or showing progress on this project.** It captures how the
4	> project owner wants images handled and how progress is visualized. These are durable rules, not a
5	> status report — for current state and next steps see [STATUS.md](STATUS.md).
6	
7	## Project in one line
8	
9	Detect and quantify the fluorescently-labeled cerebral blood vessels in the **gP-CD31 (red) confocal
10	panels** from Wang et al. 2022. The professor's three asks: **categorize, count, measure (length)**.
11	Biology + imaging numbers: [`references/wang-2022-cd31-vascular-network/digest.md`](../references/wang-2022-cd31-vascular-network/digest.md).
12	
13	**Working dataset:** every `references/*/figures/panels/VESSEL_*.png` — the isolated vessel channel,
14	one folder per source paper. The **16 Wang gP-CD31 (red) rat panels** are the primary set, the one
15	`expected-results.md` was written against and the one the results tables are built on. Panels from
16	other papers are additional inputs with their own caveats (species, marker, magnification) — see
17	each paper's `figures/panels/README.md`, and note that `measure_vessels.py` rolls regions up **per
18	paper** so the sets are never averaged together. Paper index and the intake protocol:
19	[`references/README.md`](../references/README.md).
20	
21	## How the owner wants to work on images
22	
23	1. **Expected results come from real visual inspection — "use your LLM might, not hard-coded."**
24	   When establishing what a good result looks like, actually *look* at the images and reason about
25	   them. Never invent/fabricate numbers, and never run the analysis pipeline and present its own
26	   output as if it were ground truth — that is circular. The visual, LLM-derived expectations live in
27	   [`references/wang-2022-cd31-vascular-network/figures/panels/expected-results.md`](../references/wang-2022-cd31-vascular-network/figures/panels/expected-results.md)
28	   and are the reference the automated pipeline is judged against.
29	
30	2. **We converse on visual assertions.** Progress is discussed by *overlaying the extracted data on
31	   the images* and reacting to what we see. Whenever you propose or revise the extraction, produce a
32	   visual overlay and make explicit, checkable claims ("this outline = what I call a vessel; that red
33	   vessel has no outline = the baseline missed it").
34	
35	3. **Be honest about failure modes.** The overlays are QA tools first. Show where the method breaks
36	   (missed faint vessels, fragmentation, thick-vessel handling); do not hide it or over-claim.
37	
38	4. **Metric definitions (locked):**
39	   - **COUNT = branch segments** (junction-to-junction / junction-to-tip pieces). Junctions and
40	     connected-vessel count are also reported, but the *segment* is the primary count unit.
41	   - **CATEGORIZE = vessel caliber**: capillary vs penetrating artery, by centerline diameter.
42	   - **MEASURE = total centerline length**; report both raw µm and the scale-invariant density.
43	
44	5. **Real units & cross-figure comparison.** px→µm is calibrated from the **scale bar the figure
45	   itself prints**, measured off the panel — never assumed from a stated field size. For the Wang
46	   panels every bar is 50 µm (fig1 = 0.820, fig3 = 1.064, fig4/5/6 = 0.658 µm/px); other papers print
47	   other lengths, so `SCALEBAR_PX` is keyed by panel-name prefix and `SCALEBAR_UM` carries any bar
48	   that is not 50 µm. All of it lives in `measure_vessels.py` — the single calibration source.
49	   The figures are at **different zoom**, so **raw length is NOT comparable across figures** — use
50	   **length density (mm/mm²)** and **area %** for any cross-region/cross-figure comparison.
51	
52	   **A panel with no measurable bar is declared, not guessed.** If a figure draws no scale bar, add
53	   the panel prefix to `UNCALIBRATED` with the reason instead of borrowing a neighbouring row's
54	   scale. Such panels report area % and pixels only, and drop out of every µm and density number —
55	   which is fine, as long as it is on the record rather than silent.
56	
57	6. **Commit rule for images.** Commit image files **only if** they come from real data, or we agree
58	   they are valuable as progress or ground truth. In practice:
59	   - **Rendered overlay PNGs are gitignored** (`analysis/overlays/`, `analysis/annotated/`) —
60	     regenerate them from the scripts; do not commit them without explicit agreement.
61	   - **Commit the scripts and the derived numeric results** (the markdown tables) — those are the
62	     tracked progress.
63	
64	## Visualization conventions (how we show progress)
65	
66	The annotated overlay is the standard way we look at progress. **Source of truth:**
67	[`annotate_overlays.py`](annotate_overlays.py). Regenerate:
68	`python3 analysis/annotate_overlays.py [name-substring ...]` → writes to `analysis/annotated/` (gitignored).
69	
70	The owner iterated to this exact style — keep it:
71	
72	- **Overlay on the ORIGINAL image at full brightness.** Do not dim the original.
73	- **Highlight = a slim outline that circles the detected thing — never a color fill.** "Don't add a
74	  layer of pixels over the thing you want to highlight; make it a very slim boundary."
75	- **Lines are thin and semi-transparent** so the original signal reads through them. Contours are
76	  drawn at *display* resolution (1 px, so upscaling doesn't fatten them) and alpha-blended (~0.5).
77	  Arrows and junction rings are drawn on a semi-transparent overlay (~0.4–0.7 alpha), 1 px.
78	- **Colors, chosen to contrast with the red signal:** capillary outline = **cyan**, artery outline =
79	  **green**, junction = small **magenta** hollow ring. **Avoid red for overlays** (it disappears on
80	  the red vessels).
81	- **Arrows + labels:** point an arrow at representative measured vessels and write the **length in
82	  µm**; for an example artery, write its **diameter**. Labels stay opaque/readable.
83	- **Drawn scale bar** inside the image, labelled with that panel's real bar length (50 µm for the
84	  Wang panels; other papers differ), and a **totals banner along the bottom**: segment count
85	  (capillary/artery split), total length + density, junction count, area %. An uncalibrated panel
86	  gets no overlay at all — `annotate_overlays.py` skips it and says so, rather than drawing a bar
87	  it cannot justify.
88	- **Tuning knobs** (in `annotate_overlays.py`): `CONTOUR_A` (contour opacity), `ARROW_A` / `RING_A`
89	  (arrow/ring alpha), `SC` (render scale), `ARTERY_DIAM_PX` (caliber threshold, in `measure_vessels.py`).
90	
91	## File map
92	
93	| Path | What |
94	|---|---|
95	| `references/README.md` | Index of every source paper + the intake protocol. |
96	| `references/METHODS-SYNTHESIS.md` | Cross-paper method comparison: what the literature does, what we adopted, what we rejected. |
97	| `references/<paper>/digest.md` | Self-contained digest per paper — read this instead of the PDF. |
98	| `references/<paper>/figures/` + `panels/` | Full figures and cropped panels; `VESSEL_*.png` = working-dataset inputs; each `README.md` = inventory + descriptions. |
99	| `references/wang-2022-cd31-vascular-network/figures/panels/expected-results.md` | Visual (LLM) expected results for the primary 16 panels — the validation reference. |
100	| `analysis/measure_vessels.py` | Extraction + metrics (categorize/count/measure). `--overlays` writes a 3-panel debug view. |
101	| `analysis/annotate_overlays.py` | Presentation overlays in the style above. |
102	| `analysis/results-first-pass.md` | Measured results, calibration, limitations. |
103	| `analysis/STATUS.md` | Current state and agreed next step. |
104	
105	Setup: `pip install -r requirements.txt` (numpy, scipy, scikit-image, Pillow).

1	// APPLYING a status transition — the write half of the vocabulary whose read half
2	// is `work-item.mjs`'s decode (tasks-dispatch DESIGN §4, the migration of #1119).
3	//
4	// One rule, and it is why this is not a plain `swapLabel`: the item may wear ANY
5	// engine version's spelling of the status it is leaving. A member's items outlive
6	// its converges, so an item filed as `task:ready` is picked up by an engine that
7	// writes `task:status:waiting-for-executor`, and a swap that named one spelling
8	// would leave the other standing — an item wearing two live statuses, which is the
9	// torn state the janitor exists to repair.
10	//
11	// Writes stay granular (add and remove named labels, never a set-write): with
12	// several executors and a scheduler run moving labels at once, a set-write from a
13	// stale snapshot clobbers a concurrent transition (DESIGN §4).
14	// The removes are UNCONDITIONAL — every spelling of the status being left, not
15	// only the ones the caller's snapshot shows. A caller holds the labels it read
16	// before its own earlier transitions, so filtering on that snapshot would skip
17	// exactly the label this engine just wrote; removing a label an issue does not
18	// carry 404s, which is the end state asked for and therefore success.
19	import { spellingsOf } from './work-item.mjs';
20	
21	// Move `item` out of `fromStatus` (canonical — every spelling of it goes) and into
22	// the label `to`, which is whatever spelling this engine writes.
23	export async function swapStatus(api, gh, repo, item, fromStatus, to) {
24	  await clearStatus(api, gh, repo, item, fromStatus);
25	  return api.addLabel(gh, repo, item.number, to);
26	}
27	
28	// Leave a status without entering another — the close path, where the terminal
29	// label is applied separately.
30	export async function clearStatus(api, gh, repo, item, status) {
31	  for (const label of spellingsOf(status)) {
32	    await api.removeLabel(gh, repo, item.number, label);
33	  }

content.content:
# Claude Code agent proxy

Outbound HTTPS from this session goes through a local proxy at [REDACTED:env:https_proxy]
(set via HTTPS_PROXY) which tunnels to a policy-enforcing egress proxy. TLS is
re-terminated there, so every tool must trust the CA bundle at
[REDACTED:env:NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS]. The standard CA environment variables, the system trust
store (where possible), a JVM truststore, the Bazel system bazelrc, the
browser NSS store, and gsutil's boto config are already set up.

## Quick diagnosis

1. Run: curl -sS [REDACTED:env:https_proxy]/__agentproxy/status
   It reports proxy state, which trust and git accommodations are active
   (javaTrustStorePath, toolTrustFailureCodes, gitSshRewrite,
   gitConfigConflicts), and the most recent proxy-side failures.
2. Find the failure class below and apply the matching fix; gitConfigConflicts
   codes map to the git section, toolTrustFailureCodes to the JVM section.
3. Never disable TLS verification, never unset HTTPS_PROXY, and do not retry
   organization policy denials (403/407) — report them instead.

## Failure classes and fixes

### "certificate verify failed" / "self-signed certificate in chain" / PKIX errors

The failing tool is not reading the pre-set CA configuration. In order:

- If the tool has a CA flag or env var, point it at [REDACTED:env:NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS]
  (examples: --cacert, SSL_CERT_FILE, NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS, REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE,
  AWS_CA_BUNDLE, DENO_CERT, CARGO_HTTP_CAINFO, PIP_CERT, GIT_SSL_CAINFO,
  BUNDLE_SSL_CA_CERT, HEX_CACERTS_PATH, NIX_SSL_CERT_FILE).
- Tool config files override environment variables. If one of these sets its
  own CA or disables verification, point it at the bundle instead:
  pip.conf "cert", npm "cafile" (npm config get cafile), ~/.curlrc "cacert",
  .wgetrc "ca_certificate", conda "ssl_verify", git "http.sslCAInfo",
  gradle.properties / MAVEN_OPTS "-Djavax.net.ssl.trustStore".
- JVM tools (Maven, Gradle, plain Java): when a JDK is present, a truststore
  is built at /root/.ccr/java-truststore.p12 (password "changeit") and
  injected via JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS — confirm javaTrustStorePath is set in the
  status output before pointing a build at it (toolTrustFailureCodes explains
  why it is missing). If the image or the build sets its own trustStore, that
  one wins — import the proxy CA into it with
  keytool -importcert -noprompt -alias ccr-agent-proxy -file /root/.ccr/agent-proxy-ca.crt -keystore <their store>
  or point the build at the ready-made one. Bazel reads the managed block in
  /etc/bazel.bazelrc rather than JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS.

### "405 Method Not Allowed" from the proxy

The tool sent a plain-HTTP (non-CONNECT) request: usually axios older than
1.16.1 (upgrade it) or a tool configured with HTTP_PROXY (unset HTTP_PROXY for
that tool — only HTTPS_PROXY is supported).

### 403 / 407 from the proxy

The destination host is not allowed by your organization's egress policy for
this session. Do not retry or route around it — report the blocked host.
Note: curl hides response bodies on failed CONNECTs; the status endpoint
records the reason.

### Tool ignores the proxy entirely (timeouts with no proxy error)

Some clients do not read HTTPS_PROXY: Node's built-in fetch (run that command
with NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY=1 on Node >= 22.21), aiohttp (pass trust_env=True),
Ruby bundler (reads only HTTP_PROXY, which this proxy does not serve),
hand-rolled Go dialers. Prefer the tool's own proxy option where one exists.

### git

SSH-form GitHub remotes ([REDACTED:env:GIT_CONFIG_VALUE_1]...) are rewritten to HTTPS
automatically unless this session has its own SSH setup or supplies its own
GIT_CONFIG_* (see gitSshRewrite in the status output). A gitconfig that sets
http.proxy / http.<url>.proxy (even empty), its own http.sslCAInfo, or an
https-to-ssh insteadOf makes git bypass the proxy or fail verification — the
status output's gitConfigConflicts codes name which of these were detected;
adjust those keys for this session if git times out.

### docker build / docker run

Processes inside containers cannot reach [REDACTED:env:CLOUDSDK_PROXY_ADDRESS]:43911 and do not trust
the CA. Workarounds: run builds with --network host, copy [REDACTED:env:NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS]
into the build context and install it in an early layer, and pass proxy/CA
settings explicitly to the build.

### Not supported through the proxy (report, do not work around)

gRPC / HTTP/2-only APIs, WebSocket upgrades, client-mTLS, certificate-pinned
clients (e.g. Snowflake, ngrok), non-443 HTTPS ports, raw-TCP databases.

If a tool still cannot work through the proxy, report it to your
administrator or Anthropic support so the policy or tooling can be fixed.

store (where possible), a JVM truststore, the Bazel system bazelrc, the
browser NSS store, and gsutil's boto config are already set up.

## Quick diagnosis

1. Run: curl -sS [REDACTED:env:https_proxy]/__agentproxy/status
   It reports proxy state, which trust and git accommodations are active

   gitConfigConflicts), and the most recent proxy-side failures.
2. Find the failure class below and apply the matching fix; gitConfigConflicts
   codes map to the git section, toolTrustFailureCodes to the JVM section.
3. Never disable TLS verification, never unset HTTPS_PROXY, and do not retry
   organization policy denials (403/407) — report them instead.

## Failure classes and fixes

### "certificate verify failed" / "self-signed certificate in chain" / PKIX errors

The failing tool is not reading the pre-set CA configuration. In order:

- If the tool has a CA flag or env var, point it at [REDACTED:env:NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS]
  (examples: --cacert, SSL_CERT_FILE, NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS, REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE,
  AWS_CA_BUNDLE, DENO_CERT, CARGO_HTTP_CAINFO, PIP_CERT, GIT_SSL_CAINFO,
  BUNDLE_SSL_CA_CERT, HEX_CACERTS_PATH, NIX_SSL_CERT_FILE).
- Tool config files override environment variables. If one of these sets its
  own CA or disables verification, point it at the bundle instead:
  pip.conf "cert", npm "cafile" (npm config get cafile), ~/.curlrc "cacert",
  .wgetrc "ca_certificate", conda "ssl_verify", git "http.sslCAInfo",
  gradle.properties / MAVEN_OPTS "-Djavax.net.ssl.trustStore".
- JVM tools (Maven, Gradle, plain Java): when a JDK is present, a truststore
  is built at /root/.ccr/java-truststore.p12 (password "changeit") and
  injected via JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS — confirm javaTrustStorePath is set in the
  status output before pointing a build at it (toolTrustFailureCodes explains
  why it is missing). If the image or the build sets its own trustStore, that
  one wins — import the proxy CA into it with
  keytool -importcert -noprompt -alias ccr-agent-proxy -file /root/.ccr/agent-proxy-ca.crt -keystore <their store>
  or point the build at the ready-made one. Bazel reads the managed block in
  /etc/bazel.bazelrc rather than JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS.

### "405 Method Not Allowed" from the proxy

The tool sent a plain-HTTP (non-CONNECT) request: usually axios older than
1.16.1 (upgrade it) or a tool configured with HTTP_PROXY (unset HTTP_PROXY for
that tool — only HTTPS_PROXY is supported).

### 403 / 407 from the proxy

The destination host is not allowed by your organization's egress policy for
this session. Do not retry or route around it — report the blocked host.
Note: curl hides response bodies on failed CONNECTs; the status endpoint
records the reason.

### Tool ignores the proxy entirely (timeouts with no proxy error)

Some clients do not read HTTPS_PROXY: Node's built-in fetch (run that command
with NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY=1 on Node >= 22.21), aiohttp (pass trust_env=True),
Ruby bundler (reads only HTTP_PROXY, which this proxy does not serve),
hand-rolled Go dialers. Prefer the tool's own proxy option where one exists.

### git

SSH-form GitHub remotes ([REDACTED:env:GIT_CONFIG_VALUE_1]...) are rewritten to HTTPS
automatically unless this session has its own SSH setup or supplies its own
GIT_CONFIG_* (see gitSshRewrite in the status output). A gitconfig that sets
http.proxy / http.<url>.proxy (even empty), its own http.sslCAInfo, or an
https-to-ssh insteadOf makes git bypass the proxy or fail verification — the
status output's gitConfigConflicts codes name which of these were detected;
adjust those keys for this session if git times out.

### docker build / docker run

Processes inside containers cannot reach [REDACTED:env:CLOUDSDK_PROXY_ADDRESS]:43911 and do not trust
the CA. Workarounds: run builds with --network host, copy [REDACTED:env:NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS]
into the build context and install it in an early layer, and pass proxy/CA
settings explicitly to the build.

### Not supported through the proxy (report, do not work around)

gRPC / HTTP/2-only APIs, WebSocket upgrades, client-mTLS, certificate-pinned
clients (e.g. Snowflake, ngrok), non-443 HTTPS ports, raw-TCP databases.

If a tool still cannot work through the proxy, report it to your
administrator or Anthropic support so the policy or tooling can be fixed.
